summary: Redwood AE + SE ran an SDK integration walkthrough with Apex Analytics covering Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth patterns (API key vs service account), environment setup, and quick demos of the Console and Redwood Optimize suggestions. Customer raised questions about data residency, SSO, SOC2, and dedicated vs hosted latency/cost tradeoffs. Meeting ended with agreed next steps: share code, pricing, and schedule benchmarks.
topics: Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, caching, quantization
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, AE on this account, and with me is Priya our SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Lena (Apex): Doing well, thanks. Excited to see the SDK flow, we've skimmed the docs but want the nitty gritty.
[00:12] Priya (Redwood SE): Great — we'll run through Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth patterns, env setup, and a short Console tour, then leave time for questions.
[00:20] Marcus (Apex SRE): We have a specific ask around env management and service accounts for CI, and also latency targets.
[00:27] Alex: Perfect. Quick agenda — auth, local quickstarts, deploying a route in Console, then Optimize tips (batching/caching/quant). Sound ok?
[00:33] Ravi (CTO): Yep. Also want to confirm compliance posture — SOC2 and KMS for key management.
[00:38] Priya: We'll cover that — short answer is yes, we've got SOC 2 and KMS integrations; I'll share the security pack after.
[00:44] [01:00] Priya: Ok jumping into auth. For most dev flows we recommend an API key set as an env var REDWOOD_API_KEY. Example, in bash: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxx. For CI/pipeline you can use our service accounts, which are scoped and rotated via the Console.
[01:15] Marcus: Service accounts — are those compatible with our Vault?
[01:19] Priya: Yes, you can write the key to Hashi Vault and rotate. We also support KMS-based key wrapping for private deployments. Sometimes folks mishear our product name as "Redwood Dedication" — it's Redwood Dedicated.
[01:30] Alex: We'll drop the docs link and sample terraform snippet after the call.
[01:36] [02:00] Priya: Python quickstart — minimal example:
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate("Summarize customer feedback: ...")
print(resp.text)

Priya: That's the gist; the SDK handles streaming and retries. For direct HTTP, you can also POST to /v1/generate with Authorization: Bearer <key>.
[02:28] Lena: Is there a typed Python client? we mostly use type hints and pydantic.
[02:32] Priya: The client has type annotations; we'll add a snippet for pydantic models in the repo.
[02:37] [03:00] Priya: TypeScript quickstart is similar — show an example:
import Redwood from '@redwoodai/sdk'
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const resp = await client.generate({ prompt: '...' })
console.log(resp.text)

Priya: For serverless, set the env var in your platform (Vercel, Cloud Run). For local dev we recommend a .env and dotenv.
[03:30] Marcus: Any native retry or circuit breaker in SDK? we run into 503s under bursty traffic.
[03:35] Priya: SDK has built-in retries for idempotent ops and an optional circuit breaker. For production bursts we recommend Redwood Dedicated or autoscaling config to avoid 503s.
[03:43] [04:00] Alex: Quick demo of Console — routes let you pin a model variant, set per-route batching and cache TTL, and attach a rollout policy. You can also create service accounts and API keys from the Security tab.
[04:15] Lena: Can we limit keys to only embeddings or only generation?
[04:18] Alex: Yes, scopes per key — embed-only, generate-only. We'll include a screenshot in the follow-up.
[04:25] [05:00] Priya: Now Optimize tips — first, batching: set a target batch size based on average request token length. Batching reduces per-token cost but can add a few ms of latency. Customers with conversational agents typically use small continuous batching so latency stays low.
[05:40] Priya: Second, prefix/KV cache — if you have repeated system prompts or instructions, cache those keys to avoid recomputing. Third, quantization — for some open models a 4-bit quantized variant reduces cost with minimal quality regression; we'll recommend specific quant profiles based on your eval set.
[06:10] Marcus: How do you run quantized models in hosted vs private?
[06:14] Priya: Hosted supports verified quant variants in our catalog. For Private/On-prem you can bring your own quant weights and we support the runtime, but that requires a bit more ops setup.
[06:22] [07:00] Ravi: On data residency — we need EU-only processing for a subset of customers. Is region pinning available?
[07:06] Alex: Yes, you can pin region per-route and enforce that in routing policies. For private deployments we can run in your VPC in a specific region. We'll include the region options doc.
[07:18] Lena: Any penalties for falling back to a cheaper model if capacity is constrained? example degrade gracefully.
[07:22] Priya: You can configure automatic fallback to a compatible model variant with a quality/regression guard; Console will surface fallback events and we tie those into Optimize alerts.
[07:30] [08:00] Marcus: Security checklist — SSO, SAML, RBAC, audit logs?
[08:05] Alex: Yes: SAML/SSO for Console, fine-grained RBAC, audit logs exportable to your SIEM, and we support customer-managed KMS in Private. Priya will share SOC 2/ISO artifacts.
[08:16] Priya: We sometimes see transcripters write "KMS/HSM" funny, but we do support HSM integrations for key material.
[08:22] [09:00] Priya: Quick network note — if you go Private, we provide an install bundle and the control plane can be customer-managed. For on-prem there's an air-gapped option.
[09:10] Marcus: Ok good.
[09:15] [10:00] Priya: Now a short live code demo — I'll run the Python snippet and show a small generate and streaming example. (typing sounds)
[10:25] Priya: You might see slight transcription glitches in code samples in the recording — we'll paste the repo link.
[10:30] [11:00] Alex: On pricing — hosted is usage-based; Dedicated has reserved capacity and committed terms that lower unit cost. We'll send a committed capacity example for your traffic profile.
[11:20] Ravi: What's the SLA for Dedicated?
[11:23] Alex: SLA varies by plan; typical is 99.9% with latency targets — I'll include the SLA doc.
[11:30] [12:00] Lena: For the pilot, we want to test two flows: 1) analytics summarization (short prompts, many requests) and 2) conversational assistant (longer context, lower qps).
[12:12] Priya: Good split — for summarization we'd recommend higher batching thresholds and maybe a quant variant for cost. For convo, keep smaller batches and prefix cache.
[12:20] [13:00] Marcus: On telemetry, what do the dashboards show? token-level cost? per-route latency?
[13:04] Alex: Console shows token-level cost, token counts per request, per-route latency p50/p95, and trace links for errors. You can export metrics or integrate with Datadog.
[13:13] [14:00] Lena: Any gotchas with TypeScript in Deno vs Node?
[14:05] Priya: For Deno you can use the raw fetch examples; our SDK is Node-first but we link to a Deno snippet.
[14:12] [15:00] Ravi: Are there rate-limits we should worry about during the pilot?
[15:04] Alex: We have account-level rate limits but they can be customized for pilots; we'll include burst allowances in the pilot proposal.
[15:12] [16:00] Priya: Ok quick recap of the code flow: set REDWOOD_API_KEY, install SDK, call generate/embed endpoints, use streaming client for UI. We'll include sample code for both python and ts in the repo link.
[16:25] Lena: Can you also include a small E2E example with our ingress (we use Kong) and a lambda?
[16:29] Priya: Sure — I'll add a short example showing Kong header propagation and setting env vars in lambda.
[16:34] [17:00] Alex: Security follow-up: Priya will send SOC2 docs and KMS/HSM integration notes, and I'll attach the Dedicated pricing sheet.
[17:10] Marcus: We'll also share our traffic pattern and SLOs.
[17:14] [18:00] Priya: One more Optimize tip — use a small eval set to measure quality drop when switching quant profiles. We'll help run an eval job if you want.
[18:12] Lena: That would be great.
[18:15] [19:00] Alex: Any final questions?
[19:03] Ravi: No, not now. We'll review the materials and loop back.
[19:08] Alex: Great, thanks everyone. Next steps: we'll send the repo, pricing, and security docs; schedule benchmarks.
[19:20] Lena: Thanks Alex, Priya.
[19:22] (meeting ends)
